responseText:
I'll start by pulling up both product pages.
Both are identical on specs. Next I'll read the passport sections and check them.
I'd buy **#1, the Oskvale Trailcell 500**. The two listings are almost identical, and the one real difference is that only #1's Digital Product Passport holds up.

**What's the same**
- Both cost €649 including VAT and are in stock.
- Both are 500 Wh, 36 V, 13.9 Ah NMC packs with 40 21700 cells.
- Both are rated for 720 W continuous and 1,080 W peak, and both weigh 2.9 kg.
- Both have the same down-tube rail with key lock and are rated for 800 cycles.
- Both come with a 2-year warranty, a 42 V 4 A charger, two keys, free EU delivery and 30-day returns.
- Both are sold and shipped by Oskvale Store, and neither has reviews yet.

Neither listing gives you a performance reason to pick one over the other.

**The passport check**

Both pages say the battery has an EU Digital Product Passport, but a page's own claim isn't proof. I checked each one against the public LUKSO ledger and didn't use the verify links on the pages.

- **#1, Oskvale Trailcell 500: verified.**
  - The ledger holds a record for this exact item (GTIN 09520606000019, serial 000001), named "Oskvale Trailcell 500 e-bike battery".
  - The account that issued it has the profile name "Oskvale" and still holds it.
  - Oskvale's own site declares that same account.
  - One caveat: the ledger record doesn't state which brand it belongs to. The link between the record and the brand rests on that site declaration, so I can't confirm it independently.
- **#2, Torvlund Ridgepack 500: not verified.**
  - I found no ledger record for GTIN 09520606000040, serial 000001.
  - The page's own token reference (a different collection and token ID) also returned no record.
  - The passport link on the page points to oskvale-store.com, which is the shop, not Torvlund. Its "independent record" link is on the shop's own domain too, so it isn't independent.
  - A missing record doesn't prove the battery is fake. But the page presents a passport that I couldn't back up.

**Other points**
- The EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 requires a passport for LMT batteries, which covers e-bike batteries, from February 2027. An unverifiable passport on #2 is therefore worth taking seriously.
- #1's passport lists the manufacturer's address as "Eksempelvej 1". That's Danish for "Example Street 1", which looks like a placeholder. That's a small red flag for #1 as well, so ask the seller about it.
- Oskvale Store appears to be a small shop with no reviews. Pay by card so you have chargeback protection, and use the 30-day return window.
- Before buying, check that the battery fits your bike's motor and mount. Both are 36 V with a down-tube rail, but compatibility depends on your drive system.

Tell me your bike and motor and I can help you check that.

The specs match exactly, so the battery passports are the only real difference. I'll check those records.
I'd go with **option 1, the Oskvale Trailcell 500**. The two batteries look the same on paper, but only the Trailcell's EU battery passport can be checked against sources outside the store.

**The specs and terms are identical.** Both listings show the same numbers:
- €649 with free EU delivery, 30-day returns and a 2-year warranty
- 36 V, 500 Wh (13.9 Ah), using 40 standard 21700-size cells
- The same power output, 2.9 kg weight and 800-cycle lifespan (charges before the battery drops to 80% of its capacity)
- The same charger and the same claimed range of 60–120 km

So performance, price and terms can't decide it.

**The difference is the battery passport.** Under the new EU Battery Regulation, e-bike batteries carry a digital passport showing who made the battery, where and when. A passport is only worth something if someone other than the seller vouches for it:

| | Trailcell 500 (option 1) | Ridgepack 500 (option 2) |
|---|---|---|
| Passport hosted on | The manufacturer's own website (oskvale.com) | **The store's website** (oskvale-store.com), not Torvlund's |
| Manufacturer's own statement confirming it issued the passport | Yes | **Missing** |
| "Independent record" | On a separate site (passportrecord.org) | **On the store's own website**, so not independent |
| Declaration of conformity (the maker's safety-compliance document) | On the manufacturer's website | On the store's website |
| Manufacturer address | Full street address in Copenhagen | Just "Gothenburg, Sweden" |
| Batch code vs. manufacture date | Batch "2610" fits the October 2026 date | Batch "2609" doesn't match the October 2026 date |

For the Ridgepack, every record that should prove the passport is real is hosted by the shop selling it. That doesn't prove anything is wrong, but you can't check it independently. For a lithium battery, being sure of who made it and that it meets EU safety rules really matters.

**Caveat:** I hit my lookup limit before I could open the passport pages and blockchain records themselves. This comparison is based only on what the two product pages show.

**If you want to double-check:**
- Scan the Trailcell's QR code and make sure it opens a page on oskvale.com.
- If you're still interested in the Ridgepack, ask Torvlund directly whether it issued passport GTIN 9520606000040, serial 000001, and where its official passport and conformity documents are hosted.

Neither listing has customer reviews yet, so the passport is the best way to tell them apart. Since they cost the same, I'd pick the one you can verify.
